answers.text: The nightly comparison is a job that compares the old and new engines' invoice totals per customer, flagging a mismatch when they differ by more than one cent (this is from the brief). Storing results as one row per customer per night in a comparison results table is my assumption. A failed or missing night counts as a failing day and restarts the 7-day count, because I will not let a gap pass as a clean day. Added to Terms and the failure table.

What the shadow store physically is has not been decided. Both engines read the same usage event log, which keeps entries for 35 days (from the brief). The log's technology and how each engine reads it are unknown. Marked open in the document.

The brief says a person makes forward moves and on-call starts rollbacks, but not the mechanism (command, UI or config edit). I assumed the controller computes gate status and rejects a move whose gates are not met. That is a decision to defend the word 'requires', not a verified fact. Listed as open.

The brief does not say how the rate is measured. I assumed failed charges over attempted charges in a rolling 10-minute window, checked by the controller. What counts as a failure and any minimum volume are unknown. Listed as open.

How workers and engines read billing_mode (polling, cache, push) and how fast they see a change is unknown. I changed the rollback so it does not depend on speed: the new engine checks the flag and the rollback record before every charge, and step 1 ends only when the new engine confirms it stopped. Both the new-engine behavior and the confirmation are my design additions.

The pause is the rollback record. The controller writes it in step 1, and the new engine must refuse to charge while it exists, even though billing_mode still says both or new_only. I chose this because the rules forbid changing the flag until the ledger is consistent, so the pause needs a separate signal. It is an addition to the rules and needs confirmation.

The brief says the ledger is the system of record for charges, written by the old engine in old_only and shadow, and by the new engine in both and new_only. Whether the old engine can read the new engine's ledger entries in the same format is not known. I assumed it can, keyed by customer and billing period. Listed as open.

Due now means: every customer and billing period with a finished old-engine invoice (after replay) and no charge in the ledger. That includes periods that fell due during the pause or during new_only. I chose it because the ledger check then also prevents double charges. Written into step 4. How the old engine knows a period is finished is not specified.

Day 35 counts from the stored new_only entry time (the brief says 35 days in new_only). new_only_locked is not a stored state: the controller checks the clock and refuses the rollback edge, while billing_mode stays new_only. I chose this to avoid a second source of truth. Retention matters because the old engine must reprocess skipped usage events, and the log drops events after 35 days. The oldest skipped events expire on day 35, so replay is impossible after that. Clarified in the diagram notes and open questions.

Neither the form of Finance sign-off nor the way a mismatch is resolved, or by whom, is specified in the brief. Both are listed as open. The document does say that an unresolved mismatch or missing sign-off blocks the move to new_only.

Not confirmed. The rollback record in the config service is still my assumption and needs your confirmation. If the config service is down during an automatic rollback, the controller cannot record the pause or flip the flag. I do not know what the system should do, so the document now lists it as an open question and a row in the failure table.

questions.text: How does the new engine send that confirmation, and to whom? What happens if it never confirms, or a charge is mid-send when the rollback record is written?
questions.about: Pause new charging: This step ends when the new engine confirms it has stopped

questions.text: Where does the old engine write the replayed invoices (shadow store, or somewhere else)? How does the old engine know which events it skipped, and how is pinning done on the usage event log?
questions.about: Pin and replay (from new_only only): The old engine reprocesses them and writes its invoices

questions.text: How is the 0.1 pct mismatch rate calculated: mismatched customers over customers compared, per night? Is the 5000 invoices count per night, or total over the 7 days?
questions.about: shadow --> both: 7 consecutive days under 0.1 pct mismatch and 5000+ invoices compared

questions.text: What actually blocks a forward move during a rollback: the controller rejecting the command, or something else? Who writes the "gates reset at" timestamp and when is it read?

questions.text: If a rollback starts before day 35 but the replay pin only happens in step 3 after settling in-flight charges, can the oldest skipped events expire before they are pinned? What happens then?
questions.about: new_only --> RollingBack : on-call manual or auto, only before day 35

questions.text: How does the old engine know to start charging again once the flag is old_only, given that workers read the flag at an unknown speed? Could the new engine and old engine both be reading different values for a moment?
questions.about: Set the flag to old_only. Workers see old_only only after the ledger is consistent

answers.text: Design choice, not in the brief: each new-engine instance writes an acknowledgement into the rollback record once it has seen the record and stopped charging, and the controller waits for all of them. If one never acknowledges, the controller keeps waiting, does not go on, and pages on-call; the flag is not changed. A charge that is mid-send when the record appears is handled by step 3, which waits for its outcome or looks it up by charge key. Reason: the flag cannot be changed early, so the pause needs its own confirmed signal. That instances can report this is an open assumption. Step 2 and the failure table now say this.

The old engine charges from its own finished invoice in the shadow store, and computes one from the usage events if none exists for a period. Reason: it is the old engine's own output, and recomputing everything would risk different amounts. Whether charging from a non-authoritative store is acceptable is not known, so it is listed as an open question.

Replayed invoices go to the shadow store, then step 5 charges from them. The skipped events are those since the stored new_only entry time, because the old engine stopped computing at entry. Pinning is done in step 1 on the usage event log. How the log supports pinning is unknown, so the document lists it as open.

The brief does not define this. I assumed the nightly rate is mismatched invoices over invoices compared that night, each of 7 nights must be under 0.1%, and 5,000 is the total across the 7 nights. I cannot defend per-night versus total from the brief. Now stated in Open questions.

The controller blocks it: it rejects a forward-move command while a rollback record exists and is not done, and when gates are not met. Only the controller writes the gates-reset-at timestamp, in step 6 before the flag is set, and it reads it whenever a move command or gate-status request arrives. I moved the reset into the same step as the flag so a crash cannot leave the flag at old_only with old gates. A direct flag edit in the config service would bypass the controller; whether that is prevented is unknown and now listed as open.

Yes, that was a real hole in the plan. Pinning came after pause and settle, so events from the first days of new_only could expire before they were pinned. I fixed it by moving the pin to step 1, before the pause, for rollbacks from new_only. The day-35 check applies at rollback start and a started rollback may finish. If the pin fails and events have already expired, the replay would be incomplete; what to do is unknown and listed as open.

Steps 5 and 6 are run by the controller, so the old engine does the due charges because the controller tells it to, not because it sees the flag. After the flag is old_only, the old engine charges normally with the same ledger check. A worker with a stale cached flag is the risk, so I changed the rollback record: it is no longer cleared when the flag is set. It stays, blocking the new engine, until a person moves to shadow. So a stale reader of both cannot make the new engine charge, and the shared charge key also stops duplicates. Periods that fall due between step 5 and the flag change are late but charged by the old engine's normal run. Whether both engines really use the same charge key is unverified.

questions.text: When a person moves shadow to both, the old engine must stop charging and the new engine start. What stops both from charging in the same moment while workers read the flag at different times? Is there anything like the rollback record for forward moves?
questions.about: shadow --> both : person, gates met / Who charges

questions.text: Who writes the stored new_only entry time, and when: before or after the flag is set? How does the old engine stop computing at that moment, and could it still process a few events after the entry time (so the replay overlaps)?
questions.about: both --> new_only / new_only entry time

questions.text: In step 2, how does the controller know the full list of new-engine instances that must acknowledge? What if an instance starts, scales up or restarts after the record is written?
questions.about: Pause new charging: every instance has acknowledged

questions.text: What does 'finished old-engine invoice' mean in step 5, and how does the controller tell the old engine to charge due periods? Does it send a command per customer period, or start a batch run?
questions.about: Old engine charges what is due

questions.text: The first move from old_only to shadow at initial start has no 'gates reset at' timestamp. What does the controller use as the start of the count then? And after a rollback, does the nightly comparison keep running during old_only?
questions.about: Gate counters / old_only --> shadow : gate counters start at zero

questions.text: What is the charge key's billing period when a customer is charged for a period that was split across engines? Can one customer have more than one charge per period (for example usage-based top-ups), and would the key then block a legitimate second charge?
questions.about: Charge key: customer plus billing period

answers.text: Nothing in the old plan stopped it; that was a hole. I added a handoff record for the shadow to both move, mirroring the rollback pause: the controller writes it, the old engine must check it before every charge, every registered old-engine instance acknowledges it stopped, in-flight charges settle, and only then is the flag set to both. For a short time nobody charges, and the new engine's normal run charges whatever fell due (late, not lost). The record stays during both so a stale cached shadow flag cannot make the old engine charge. Reason: the flag cannot be assumed to reach all workers at once, and the charge key and ledger check alone are only a backstop. This is an addition to the brief and needs confirmation. Added a Forward moves section.

The controller writes the new_only entry time before it sets the flag. The old engine stops computing when it sees the flag, so it may process a few events after the entry time; the stored time is therefore never later than the first skipped event. Replay may overlap those events and that is harmless, because invoices are keyed by customer and period and a replayed invoice overwrites the earlier one. An entry time slightly early only makes the day-35 limit slightly stricter. Reason: choosing a time that can only be early removes the risk of a gap. Written into the state section and rollback step 4.

The controller waits for the instances in an instance registry: each engine instance registers and sends a heartbeat. An instance that starts or restarts after the rollback record exists checks the record before charging, so it starts blocked and needs no acknowledgement. An instance whose heartbeat expires is dropped from the wait. Reason: without a list the controller cannot know when everyone has stopped. Whether the engines can register and heartbeat, or whether a registry exists, is not known; this is an assumption listed in Terms and the open questions.

A closed billing period is one whose period has ended (as the old engine already defines it). A finished invoice is one the old engine has computed in full for such a period and saved in the shadow store. The controller does not send per-period commands: it starts one batch charge-due run of the old engine, which finds the due periods itself, checks the ledger for each, and charges once with the charge key. The controller waits for the run to finish and restarts it if it crashes; it is safe to repeat. Reason: one batch with a per-period ledger check is simpler and idempotent. How the old engine decides a period is closed is not known and is listed as open. Written into step 5.

The controller writes the gates-reset-at timestamp when a person moves old_only to shadow, including the very first move, so the count always starts at that move. Step 6 of a rollback also writes it, which resets the clocks if a crash left things in between. The nightly comparison does not run in old_only because the new engine is off and there is nothing to compare, so those nights produce no rows and do not count. Reason: the count must start when comparison data can first exist. Added to the Forward moves section, Terms and the state section.

Decided part: a billing period is charged whole by one engine, whichever is charging when it falls due, because both engines read the same usage events and compute the full period; a period is never split across engines for charging, and the ledger check stops the other engine charging it again. Unknown part: whether a customer can have more than one legitimate charge per period (for example usage top-ups). The brief says never charge twice for a billing period, so I assumed one charge per customer per period; if that is wrong the charge key would block a legitimate second charge. I cannot defend the assumption from the brief, so it is marked in Terms and the open questions.

questions.text: Is the rollback record written before step 1 or only in step 2? If it exists during step 1, the new engine is already blocked, so how does step 1 not affect charging?
questions.about: Rollback steps: the controller writes the rollback record at the start / Step 1 'does not affect charging'

questions.text: What if an instance's heartbeat expires because of a network problem but the instance is still running and charging? Does anything stop it, or could it charge after the controller moves on?
questions.about: Pause new charging: An instance whose heartbeat expires is dropped from the wait

questions.text: What happens if on-call starts a rollback from shadow while a shadow to both handoff is half done (handoff record written, flag still shadow)? Which procedure wins, and what happens to the handoff record?
questions.about: Rollback steps: A manual start while one is running is a no-op / shadow to both handoff

questions.text: Who does the 'release the pins' work and how? And if the controller crashes after setting the flag but before marking the record done, what does resume do?
questions.about: Reset gates and set the flag to old_only: marks the rollback record 'done'

questions.text: In both and new_only, what does the new engine need from the old engine, and what does the nightly comparison do once the old engine stops computing in new_only? Does the comparison stop there too?
questions.about: both to new_only: The old engine stops computing when it sees the flag

questions.text: The new engine's charges in the ledger: in step 5, how does the old engine learn that a new-engine charge is still in flight or unknown if step 3 found an outcome by charge key? Is the ledger updated with the looked-up outcome, and by whom?
questions.about: Old engine charges what is due: no charge in the ledger

answers.text: The record is written when the rollback starts, before step 1, so the new engine is blocked from the start and my old claim that step 1 does not affect charging was wrong. I kept the early write because it is simpler (one record, one moment) and charges delayed by it are late, not lost. Step 1 now says it does not wait for any instance, and step 2 is the step that confirms the block. Fixed the intro, steps 1 and 2, the diagram notes and the state section.

That was a real hole. I added a lease: an instance may charge only if it read the config service successfully within the lease period, otherwise it stops by itself. The heartbeat expiry must be longer than the lease, so by the time the controller drops an instance, a partitioned instance has already stopped. The charge key and ledger check are a backstop. Added to Terms, step 2, the failure table and the open questions. Whether engines can enforce a lease, and the lease and heartbeat lengths, are unknown.

The rollback wins. The controller abandons the unfinished handoff and starts the rollback. The handoff record stays so the old engine remains blocked, and rollback step 5 deletes it before the old-engine charge-due run. Step 2 does nothing from shadow, and step 3 still settles old-engine in-flight charges. Reason: rollback is the safety path and must always be available. Written into Forward moves and the failure table.

The controller releases the pins, by removing the pin it placed in step 1 on the usage event log. How the log supports releasing a pin is unknown (open question on pinning). Step 6 is written so every action is safe to repeat. If the controller crashes after the flag is set but before 'done', it resumes from the stored step 6 and runs it again, so it rewrites the same actions, releases the pins and marks 'done'. Forward moves stay rejected until 'done'. Rewriting the gates-reset timestamp slightly later is harmless.

The new engine needs nothing from the old engine in either mode. The old engine's invoices in both exist only for the nightly comparison and for rollback. Once the old engine stops computing in new_only there is nothing to compare, so the comparison stops at the move to new_only. It was already stated in Terms as running only in shadow and both. I made the reason explicit in Terms and the new_only bullet.

Step 3 now ends only when every charge the provider confirms has a ledger row, so step 5 sees a complete ledger. A looked-up outcome that is missing from the ledger gets its row written before moving on. Who writes the missing row (controller, or the new engine's recovery routine) I do not know, because the new engine owns ledger writes in these modes; this is an open question. Backstop: the shared charge key makes the provider refuse a second charge for the same customer and period. That the old engine's charge key matches the new engine's is still unverified.

questions.text: The old engine must check that billing_mode allows it before every charge. In step 5 the flag still says both or new_only. How is the charge-due run allowed to charge then?
questions.about: Rollback step 5: delete the handoff record, then start the charge-due run

questions.text: In new_only the old engine skips events until it sees the flag old_only. Usage events keep arriving during steps 1 to 5. Which engine processes those events, and how do they get into old-engine invoices before step 6?
questions.about: Rollback step 4 Replay / step 6 set the flag to old_only

questions.text: Does the pin cover events that arrive after the pin is placed, or only events that exist at that moment? Which events does replay cover, and up to what point?
questions.about: Rollback step 1: Pin every usage event from the stored new_only entry time onward

questions.text: After the flag is old_only, how does the old engine start computing and charging again as normal? What starts it, and where does it resume from?
questions.about: Rollback step 6 and old_only after a rollback

answers.text: That was a hole. I added an 'Engine rules' section: the old engine may charge only with a valid lease, no handoff record, and flag old_only or shadow, with one exception. The charge-due run, which the controller starts at step 5, is accepted while the rollback record is at step 5, even though the flag still says both or new_only. Reason: the flag must not change until the ledger is consistent, so charging before the flag needs its own authorisation, and the rollback record is the signal I already use. This is an addition to the brief. Whether the old engine can be changed to accept such a run is unknown and is now an open question.

Also a hole: nothing processed those events. Now the old engine resumes computing when the rollback record reaches step 4. It replays from the new_only entry time to the current end of the log, then keeps processing new events live into the shadow store until the flag is old_only. Step 4 ends only when it reports it has caught up. So events that arrived during steps 1 to 3 are covered by replay, and later ones are processed live before step 5. How the old engine reports 'caught up' is unknown and listed in the open questions.

The pin is assumed to cover only events that exist when it is placed. That is enough, because later events are younger than the pinned ones and cannot expire before the rollback ends. Replay covers from the stored new_only entry time to the live end of the log, and then the old engine follows the log live. Step 1 now says this. Whether the log supports pinning, and how, is unknown and stays an open question.

Nothing has to start the old engine. It has been computing since step 4, or never stopped when coming from shadow or both. When a worker re-reads the flag and sees old_only, the normal Engine rules let it charge, so its ordinary runs resume, from the position it already holds in the log (the live end after replay). Each run charges closed periods with no ledger row, using the same ledger check and charge key. I added this paragraph to step 6. How fast workers see the flag is still unknown.

teachbacks.text:
1. Starting state. The rollout state is one global flag, `billing_mode`, in the config service. It starts at `old_only`. In that mode the old engine computes invoices, charges through the payment provider and writes the billing ledger. The new engine is off.

2. Forward move 1 (`old_only` to `shadow`). A person sends a move command to the controller. The controller records a "gates reset at" timestamp, so the gate counters start at zero. If a rollback record exists, it deletes it. Then it sets the flag to `shadow`. The old engine still charges. The new engine now reads the same usage events and computes invoices into the shadow store. It never charges and never writes the ledger. Errors in the new engine are only recorded.

3. Nightly comparison. Each night a job compares the two engines' invoice totals per customer. A difference of more than one cent is a mismatch. It saves one result row per customer per night. A failed or missing comparison counts as a failing day, and a person is alerted. The controller computes the gate counters from these rows. The document says only that they are counted from the "gates reset at" timestamp.

4. Gate check for `shadow` to `both`. A person sends the move command. The controller computes the gates from the stored rows. The gates are 7 consecutive days under 0.1% mismatch and 5000 or more invoices compared. Under the document's assumption the 5000 is a total across the 7 nights. If the gates are not met, it rejects the command. It also rejects any forward move while a rollback record exists whose step is not "done".

5. Handoff (`shadow` to `both`). The controller writes the handoff record. The old engine must check before every charge that the mode allows it and that no handoff record exists. The controller waits for every registered old-engine instance to acknowledge that it stopped charging. If one does not, it keeps waiting and pages on-call, and the flag stays `shadow`. Then it settles the old engine's in-flight charges, in the same way as rollback step 3. Then it writes the `both` entry time and sets the flag to `both`. The handoff record stays while the mode is `both`. Charges that fall due during the handoff are late, not lost. The new engine charges them in its normal run, after a ledger check.

6. Running in `both`. The new engine charges and writes the ledger. It charges only when the flag says `both` and no rollback record exists. The old engine computes into the shadow store without charging, so rollback stays cheap. The nightly comparison continues. Every charge goes to the payment provider with the charge key (customer plus billing period) as the idempotency key.

7. Forward move 3 (`both` to `new_only`). This needs 14 days in `both` with no unresolved mismatches, plus Finance sign-off. The controller writes the `new_only` entry time and then sets the flag. The old engine stops computing when it sees the flag, so the nightly comparison stops. After 35 days in `new_only`, rollback is refused (`new_only_locked`). The mode then still reads `new_only`, and the controller just refuses the rollback request. A person can then decommission the old engine.

8. Starting a rollback. A rollback can be started in three ways.
   - On-call starts it by hand from `shadow`, `both` or `new_only`.
   - It starts automatically if the charge failure rate is above 2% in any 10-minute window. This applies in `both` and `new_only`.
   - If a handoff is unfinished, a rollback abandons the handoff. The handoff record is left in place, so the old engine stays blocked.

   Only one rollback runs at a time. A second start is a no-op. The controller writes the rollback record before step 1, and from that moment the new engine is blocked from charging. The controller updates the record's step after each step.

9. Rollback step 1, pin (from `new_only` only). The controller pins all usage events since the `new_only` entry time, so the 35-day retention cannot expire them. A failure is retried. From `shadow` or `both` this step is skipped.

10. Rollback step 2, pause. Each new-engine instance sees the record, stops charging and writes an acknowledgement into the record. The controller waits for every instance in the registry that has a live heartbeat. Instances that restart after the record exists start blocked. An instance whose heartbeat expires is dropped from the wait. This is safe because the lease means it stops charging on its own, and the heartbeat expiry is longer than the lease. If a live instance does not acknowledge, the controller keeps waiting and pages on-call. It never goes on without it. The flag is not changed yet.

11. Rollback step 3, settle. Charges already sent to the provider are waited on until they have a known outcome. Unknown outcomes are looked up at the provider by charge key and are not resubmitted. If the provider confirms a charge that the ledger lacks, the missing row is written. The step ends when every confirmed charge has a ledger row.

12. Rollback step 4, replay (from `new_only` only). The old engine reprocesses the pinned events and writes invoices to the shadow store. An invoice is keyed by customer and billing period, so a replayed invoice overwrites an earlier one. A failure retries the same step.

13. Rollback step 5, old engine charges what is due. The controller deletes the handoff record if one exists. It then starts a batch "charge-due run" of the old engine and waits for it. A crashed run is restarted and is safe to repeat. For each closed period that has a finished old-engine invoice and no ledger charge, the old engine checks the ledger. If the new engine already charged that period, it skips it. Otherwise it charges once using the charge key. If there is no invoice, it computes one from the usage events first.

14. Rollback step 6, reset and flip. In this order: write the "gates reset at" timestamp, clear the `new_only` and `both` entry times, and set the flag to `old_only`. Then release the pins and mark the rollback record "done". Every action is safe to repeat. A controller crash resumes from the stored step. The record is not deleted, so the new engine stays blocked. Forward moves are rejected until the record says "done". A person then has to move `old_only` to `shadow` again, which deletes the record, and the 7-day count restarts at zero.

15. Failure handling in general. A failed rollback step is retried in place and the rollout stays in `RollingBack`. On-call is paged if retries keep failing. A controller crash resumes from the stored step. An instance that loses contact with the config service stops charging by its lease. After its heartbeat expires, the controller stops waiting for it. After day 35 with a failure rate above 2%, there is no rollback, so it is treated as an incident and fixed forward.
gaps: How a person issues a forward move (command, UI or config edit) is not specified. Whether editing the flag directly, which would bypass the gate check and handoff, is prevented is unknown.
Who the on-call person is, and how they start a rollback, is not specified.

How the flag is read by workers and engines (caching, refresh interval) is unknown. So is whether the engines can register, send heartbeats, write acknowledgements and enforce the lease. The lease and heartbeat lengths are also unknown.
The acknowledgement timeout, retry limits and the retry count that triggers paging are not given.
What counts as a charge failure (declines versus provider errors) and any minimum volume before the 2% rule applies are not defined. It is also unclear how the controller gets the charge counts.
It is unclear whether the 5,000 invoice minimum is per night or a total over the 7 nights. The document only gives an assumption.
It is unclear whether a new mismatch in `both` restarts the 14-day clock.
How Finance sign-off is recorded, and who resolves a mismatch and how, are not specified.
Who writes a missing ledger row in rollback step 3 (the controller, the new engine's recovery routine or something else) is undecided.

Whether the usage event log supports pinning and releasing pins, and how, is unknown. What to do if pinned events have already expired, or the pin fails near day 35, so that replay would be incomplete, is not decided.
How the old engine identifies 'events since `new_only` began' beyond the stored entry time is not described.

How the old engine decides a billing period is closed is unknown. It is also unknown whether one charge per customer per period is always valid, since usage top-ups would be blocked by the charge key.
Whether the old engine may charge from its non-authoritative shadow-store invoice, or must always recompute, is undecided.
The ledger format is unverified. It is unknown whether the old engine can read the new engine's charges, and whether both engines use the same charge key.
What happens when the config service is unavailable, for example when an automatic rollback fires, is not decided beyond instances stopping charging after their lease runs out.

teachbacks.text:
I will follow one request through the system: an automatic rollback from `new_only`, started because the charge failure rate went above 2% in a 10-minute window. I add the forward handoff first, because the rollback depends on the same ideas.

**Background (what I understood the pieces to be)**

- The old engine and the new engine both read the same usage event log, which keeps entries for 35 days.
- Exactly one engine is supposed to charge customers at any moment.
- `billing_mode` is one global flag in the config service. It has four values: `old_only`, `shadow`, `both` and `new_only`. Only the controller writes it.
- In `old_only` and `shadow` the old engine charges and writes the ledger. In `both` and `new_only` the new engine does.
- The ledger is the record of what was charged. The shadow store holds invoices from whichever engine is not charging.
- Two small records sit next to the flag in the config service. The rollback record blocks the new engine. The handoff record blocks the old engine.
- Each engine checks these rules itself before every charge. It may charge only if its lease is valid, meaning it has read the config service recently. If it cannot reach the config service, it stops charging on its own.
- Charge key: customer plus billing period. It is sent to the payment provider as an idempotency key, so a second charge for the same key is refused.

**The forward path, briefly**

1. A person sends a move command to the controller. The controller works out the gates from the nightly comparison results since the "gates reset at" timestamp. It rejects the command if the gates are not met. It also rejects any forward move while a rollback record exists whose step is not "done".
2. `old_only` to `shadow`: nobody's charging changes. The controller writes the "gates reset at" timestamp, deletes the rollback record if there is one, then sets the flag.
3. `shadow` to `both` is where the charger changes from old to new.
   - The controller checks the gates once, then writes the handoff record. That blocks the old engine.
   - It waits for every registered old-engine instance to acknowledge that it stopped charging. If one does not, it keeps waiting and pages on-call, and the flag stays `shadow`.
   - It settles in-flight old-engine charges, writes the `both` entry time, then sets the flag to `both`.
   - A person can cancel the handoff while the flag is still `shadow`. That deletes the handoff record and the old engine charges again.
4. `both` to `new_only`: the controller writes the `new_only` entry time, then sets the flag. The old engine stops computing when it sees the flag.

**The rollback (my main walkthrough, starting from `new_only`)**

5. **Trigger.** The controller measures the charge failure rate. On `both` or `new_only`, a rate above 2% in any 10-minute window starts an automatic rollback. On-call can also start one by hand. From `new_only` this is allowed only before day 35 since the stored `new_only` entry time. After day 35 the controller refuses the rollback and it is treated as an incident to fix forward. If a rollback is already running, a manual start is a no-op and an automatic start does nothing.
6. **Write the rollback record.** Before any step, the controller writes the rollback record into the config service. From that moment the new engine is blocked from charging. The record holds the current step and the new engines' acknowledgements. The flag still says `new_only`.
7. **Step 1, pin events (only from `new_only`).** The controller pins the usage events from the `new_only` entry time onward, so the 35-day retention cannot expire them. The pin step is retried if it fails. Newer events need no pin. If events have already expired, the document says replay cannot be complete and that this is not decided.
8. **Step 2, pause new charging.** Each new-engine instance sees the record and writes an acknowledgement into it. The controller waits for every instance in the instance registry that has a live heartbeat.
   - An instance that starts after the record exists starts blocked and needs no acknowledgement.
   - An instance whose heartbeat expires is dropped from the wait. That is safe because the lease is shorter than the heartbeat expiry, so it has already stopped charging.
   - If a live instance never acknowledges, the controller keeps waiting and pages on-call. It never goes on.
   - The flag does not change in this step.
9. **Step 3, settle in-flight charges.** Charges already sent to the payment provider must reach a known outcome. If an outcome is unknown, look it up at the provider by its charge key. Do not resubmit. Every charge the provider confirms must have a ledger row. A missing row is written before moving on. Who writes it is an open question.
10. **Step 4, replay (from `new_only` only).**
    - The controller sets the record to step 4. The old engine then computes again: it reprocesses the pinned events from the `new_only` entry time up to the current end of the log, then keeps processing new events live. Its invoices go to the shadow store.
    - Replaying events the old engine already handled is harmless, because an invoice is keyed by customer and billing period and a replayed invoice overwrites the earlier one.
    - The old engine reports when it has caught up with the live end of the log. If it cannot, the step retries and the rollback does not go on.
11. **Step 5, old engine charges what is due.**
    - The controller deletes the handoff record if one exists. It sets the record to step 5 and starts one batch "charge-due run" of the old engine, then waits for it to finish.
    - The old engine accepts this run even though the flag still says `new_only`, because the rollback record is at step 5.
    - The run finds every closed billing period that has a finished old-engine invoice and no ledger charge. If there is no invoice, it computes one from the usage events.
    - For each period it checks the ledger first. If the new engine already charged it, it skips it. Otherwise it charges once, using the charge key. A crashed run is restarted, and repeating it is safe.
12. **Step 6, reset and set the flag.**
    - In this order: write a new "gates reset at" timestamp, clear the stored `new_only` and `both` entry times, then set the flag to `old_only`.
    - Then release the pins and mark the rollback record "done".
    - Every action here is safe to repeat. If the controller crashes, it resumes from the stored step and runs the whole step again.
    - The rollback record is not deleted. It stays, and the new engine stays blocked, until a person moves `old_only` to `shadow`. That move deletes it.
13. **After the flag says `old_only`.** Nothing needs to start the old engine, because it has been computing since step 4. Once a worker re-reads the flag, the normal rule lets it charge again. It continues from the live end of the log and charges closed periods that have no ledger row, with the same ledger check and charge key. Any charges that fell due between step 5 and the flag change are late but not lost.
14. **Rollback from `shadow` or `both`.** It skips steps 1 and 4, because the old engine never stopped computing. Step 2 does nothing in `shadow`, because the new engine never charged. If a handoff was unfinished, the rollback wins: the controller abandons the handoff but leaves the handoff record in place, so the old engine stays blocked until step 5 deletes it.

**Failures, as the document gives them**

- Any rollback step that fails is retried in place. The rollout stays in `RollingBack`, new charging stays paused, and the flag is not set until the ledger is consistent. On-call is paged if retries keep failing.
- If the controller crashes mid-rollback, it resumes from the stored step.
- An instance that loses contact with the config service stops charging by itself under the lease. When contact returns, it reads the records before charging again.
- If the new engine errors in `shadow`, that is only recorded.
- A failed or missing nightly comparison counts as a failing day and restarts the 7-day count.

**Why the design avoids double charges and dropped charges**

- Each switch uses a record that engines must acknowledge before the flag changes. The ledger check and the charge key cover retries and unknown outcomes.
- Charges that fall due during a pause are late, not lost.

How workers cache and refresh the flag, the records, the instance registry and the lease is unknown. The lease and heartbeat lengths are unknown, and so is whether the engines can register, send heartbeats, write acknowledgements and enforce the lease.

Whether the old engine can be changed to accept the controller-started charge-due run and to resume computing at rollback step 4 is unknown. Without that change there is no way to charge before the flag changes.

Whether the old engine may charge from its own non-authoritative shadow-store invoice in step 5, or must always recompute, is not decided.
What the system should do if the config service is down (for example when an automatic rollback fires) is not decided beyond instances stopping charging after the lease runs out.
The physical storage of the shadow store and the nightly comparison results is not decided.
How Finance sign-off is recorded, and who resolves a mismatch and how, are not specified. Whether a new mismatch restarts the 14-day `both` clock is unclear.
Whether the 5,000 invoices compared is per night or a total over the 7 nights is unclear. The document assumes a total.
How decommissioning is done is outside the plan.

teachbacks.text:
1. Setup. Two billing engines (old and new) both read the usage event log, which keeps entries 35 days. One global flag, `billing_mode`, in the config service says which mode applies: old_only, shadow, both, new_only. Only the engine named by the mode charges. The ledger is the system of record for charges. The payment provider refuses a second charge for the same charge key (customer plus billing period). Every engine instance registers in the instance registry and sends heartbeats. By the lease, an instance may charge only if it has recently read the flag and the records and sent a heartbeat. If it loses contact with the config service, it stops charging by itself.

2. Start of the rollout (old_only to shadow). A person sends a move command to the controller. The controller writes a "gates reset at" timestamp, so the gate counters start at zero. It deletes any rollback record, then sets the flag to `shadow`. Nobody's charging changes. The old engine still charges and writes the ledger. The new engine now computes invoices from the same usage events into the shadow store. It never charges.

3. Gate checking in shadow. Each night the nightly comparison compares the two engines' invoice totals per customer and saves one row per customer per night. A mismatch is a total that differs by more than one cent. The controller does not store gate counters. It computes them from those rows, counting from the "gates reset at" timestamp. The gate for moving on is 7 consecutive days under 0.1% mismatch and 5,000 or more invoices compared. A failed or missing comparison counts as a failing day and restarts the 7-day count, and a person is alerted. New-engine errors in shadow are only recorded.

4. Forward move shadow to both (handoff).
   a. A person sends the command. The controller checks the gates once and rejects the command if they are not met. It also rejects it if a rollback record exists whose step is not "done".
   b. The controller writes the handoff record, which sits in the config service next to the flag. From then on the old engine may not charge. The flag is still `shadow`, so both engines keep computing and the comparison keeps running. Nobody charges.
   c. Each live old-engine instance sees the record, stops charging and writes an acknowledgement under its instance id. The controller repeatedly re-reads the record and the registry until the live old-engine instances are a subset of those that acknowledged. Instances that are not live are dropped from the wait, which the document says is safe because of the lease. Instances that start after the record exists check it first and need no acknowledgement. If a live instance has not acknowledged after a timeout, the controller keeps waiting and pages on-call. The flag does not change.
   d. The controller settles in-flight old-engine charges, "as in rollback step 3". It waits for each charge already sent to the provider to reach a known outcome, looking up unknown ones by charge key, and does not resubmit them blindly.
   e. The controller writes the `both` entry time, then sets the flag to `both`. The new engine now charges and writes the ledger, provided the flag is `both` or `new_only`, no rollback record exists and its lease is valid. The old engine switches to computing into the shadow store without charging. The handoff record stays for the whole of `both`, so an old worker with a stale cached `shadow` flag still cannot charge. Charges due during the handoff are late, not lost. The new engine charges them in its normal run after a ledger check.
   f. Cancelling. If the flag is still `shadow`, a person can send a cancel command. The controller deletes the handoff record and the old engine charges again. Once the flag is `both`, only a rollback undoes the move.

5. In both. The nightly comparison continues. The old engine keeps its shadow-store invoices current so rollback stays cheap.

6. Forward move both to new_only. A person sends the command. The gates are 14 days in `both` with no unresolved mismatches, and Finance sign-off. The controller writes the `new_only` entry time, then sets the flag. The same engine keeps charging. The old engine stops computing when it sees the flag, so the comparison stops.

7. Day 35 lock. Thirty-five days after the stored `new_only` entry time, rollback edges are simply refused. `billing_mode` still says `new_only`. A rollback that started before day 35 may finish. After that a person may decommission the old engine. This is an action, not a stored mode, and how it is done is outside the plan. A failure rate above 2% from day 35 on is treated as an incident and fixed forward.

8. What triggers a rollback. On-call can start one by hand from shadow, both, or new_only before day 35. An automatic rollback fires from `both` or `new_only` when the charge failure rate is above 2% in any 10-minute window. Only one rollback runs at a time. A second manual start is a no-op, and an automatic start does nothing if one is already in progress. If a handoff is unfinished, the rollback wins. The handoff is abandoned but its record stays, so the old engine stays blocked until step 5.

9. Rollback begins. Before step 1 the controller writes the rollback record, which holds the current step and the new-engine acknowledgements. From that moment the new engine may not charge. The controller updates the step after each step finishes. If a step fails, it is retried in place. Forward moves are rejected until the record says "done". If the controller crashes, it resumes from the stored step, and every step is safe to repeat. Page on-call if retries keep failing.

10. Step 1, pin (from new_only only). The controller pins usage events from the `new_only` entry time onward so the 35-day retention cannot expire them. It does not wait for any instance. From shadow or both this step is skipped. If the pin fails, it retries. If the events have already expired, the replay cannot be complete, and the document says that case is not decided.

11. Step 2, confirm the pause. Each live new-engine instance writes an acknowledgement into the rollback record once it has seen the record and stopped. The controller waits for all live instances to acknowledge. Instances that start later check the record first and so start blocked. Non-live instances are dropped, which the document says is safe because the heartbeat expiry is longer than the lease. If a live instance does not acknowledge after a timeout, the controller keeps waiting and pages on-call, and never goes on. `billing_mode` is not changed yet. In shadow this step does nothing.

12. Step 3, settle in-flight charges. The controller waits for every charge already sent to the provider to reach a known outcome, and looks up unknown ones by charge key. The step ends only when every charge the provider confirms has a ledger row. If a confirmed charge has no ledger row, the missing row is written before moving on.

13. Step 4, replay (from new_only only). The controller sets the rollback record to step 4. From then on the old engine computes again. It reprocesses the pinned events from the `new_only` entry time to the current end of the log, then keeps processing live. Its invoices go to the shadow store. An invoice is keyed by customer and billing period, so replaying over events it already handled just overwrites and is harmless. The step ends when the old engine reports it has caught up with the live end of the log. If it cannot catch up, the step is retried and step 5 does not start. From shadow or both this step is skipped.

14. Step 5, old engine charges what is due. First the controller deletes the handoff record if one exists. Then it sets the rollback record to step 5 and starts a one-off charge-due run of the old engine, which waits for it to finish. The old engine accepts this run only while the rollback record is at step 5, even though the flag still says `both` or `new_only`. The run finds closed billing periods that have a finished old-engine invoice and no ledger charge. If there is no invoice, it computes one from the usage events. For each period it checks the ledger first. If the new engine already charged, it skips the period. Otherwise it charges once with the charge key. A crashed run is restarted and is safe to repeat.

15. Step 6, reset and set the flag. In order, the controller writes a new "gates reset at" timestamp, clears the stored `new_only` and `both` entry times, and sets the flag to `old_only`. Then it releases the pins and marks the rollback record "done". If the controller crashes, it reruns the whole step, which is safe. The rollback record is not deleted. It stays, and the new engine stays blocked, until a person moves `old_only` to `shadow`. That move deletes it, so a person must go back through shadow.

16. After old_only. Workers re-read the flag and see `old_only`. The old engine's normal rules then let it charge, so it resumes its ordinary runs from its current position in the log. Each ordinary run charges closed periods with no ledger row, using the same ledger check and charge key. The new engine is off.

17. Other failures. An instance that loses contact with the config service stops charging after its lease runs out, and when contact returns it reads the records before charging again. An instance that is in the registry but never sends a heartbeat is not waited for, and on-call is alerted. A controller crash mid-handoff resumes from the handoff record, and nobody charges until the move finishes or a person cancels it. If the config service is unavailable, instances stop charging after their lease runs out, and the document does not decide anything beyond that.
